extraction_text: The speaker explains various names and identities attributed to them throughout mythology.
Krishna states they were called 'Ape-Bull' by Prajapati Kashyapa because the ape is the best animal and dharma is the bull.
Krishna claims to be the world's ruler and witness, unknown in beginning, middle, or end by gods and asuras, thus called 'Beginningless, Endless, Middleless'.
Krishna explains being named 'Clean-Hearing' because they listen to pure words and reject evil ones.
Krishna recounts transforming into a miraculous unicorn boar to pull out the submerged earth, earning the name 'Unicorn'.
During the boar incarnation, having three humps led to the name 'Three-Humped'.
Followers of Kapila's doctrine call Krishna 'Purifier', and as Prajapati, they create all worlds from the heart.
Samkhya philosophers call Krishna 'Kapila', eternally established in the sun with knowledge as assistant.
Krishna identifies as the radiant golden embryo praised in hymns and worshipped by yogis.
Vedic scholars call Krishna the Rigveda with 21 branches and Samaveda with 1000 branches, chanted in forest texts by rare Brahmanas.
For sacrificing priests, Krishna is the Yajurveda with 101 branches.
Brahmanas versed in Atharvaveda call Krishna the Atharvaveda with five rituals and various potent spells.
Krishna claims to have created all Vedic branches, songs, phonemes, syllables, and accents.
Krishna appeared as Horse-Head, granting favors, and appears in Vedic appendices, knowing Vedic recitation.
Through Krishna's favor, noble Panchala followed Rama (Parashurama)'s path and obtained Vedic recitation; Bābhravya sage first mastered it.
Karala sage, blessed by Narayana, attained supreme yoga, compiled and taught Vedic recitation.
Gandharika and mighty Brahmadatta repeatedly recalled the pain of birth and death, excelled in seven births, and achieved yogic accomplishment.
Krishna states they once became Dharma's son for a special reason, thus named 'Dharma-born'.
Nara and Narayana, following dharma, ascended Mount Gandhamadana to practice eternal austerities.
During Daksha's sacrifice, he did not allow Rudra a share of offerings.
Following Dadhichi's words, Rudra destroyed Daksha's sacrifice and angrily threw a perpetually burning trident.
After reducing Daksha's great sacrifice to ashes, the trident flew to Nara and Narayana's jujube hermitage and fell on Narayana's chest.
Narayana's hair turned Munja grass color from the impact, giving Krishna the name 'Munja-kesha'.
Great-souled Narayana uttered 'Om', causing the trident to fly back to Shankara (Rudra).
Rudra then ran toward the two powerful sages.
Narayana grabbed Rudra by the neck, causing Rudra's neck to turn blue, earning him the name Nilakantha (Blue-Throated).
Nara took a reed, chanted a mantra, and transformed it into a great axe, which he threw at Rudra, but it shattered upon impact.
Arjuna asks Krishna who won the battle that destroyed the three worlds.

Krishna describes the cosmic battle between Rudra and Narayana, which caused universal chaos: fire rejected offerings, Vedas hid, darkness prevailed, earth shook, sky vanished, luminaries dimmed, Brahma fell, oceans dried, and mountains cracked.

Brahma, accompanied by gods and sages, intervenes and pleads with Rudra to stop for the world's welfare, explaining that Narayana and Nara are manifestations of the same supreme being, and Rudra himself originated from that being's anger.

attributes.relationship: Brahma as mediator, Rudra and Narayana/Nara as manifestations of the same source

extraction_text: Rudra calms his anger, seeks forgiveness from Narayana, and takes refuge in Hari.

Hari (Narayana) forgives Rudra, declares their unity ('who knows you, knows me'), and they exchange auspicious marks: Hari receives a trident mark as a swastika on his chest, and Rudra gets a finger-mark, earning the title Shankara.
Nara, Narayana, and Rudra form an unparalleled friendship, dismiss the gods, and resume their ascetic practices peacefully.

attributes.action: Friendship formation and return to asceticism

extraction_text: Krishna concludes by telling Arjuna that Narayana won the battle, explains the origins of his mystical names, and assures Arjuna of his protection in war.

attributes.relationship: Divine guide and protector to warrior

extraction_text: The speaker (likely Janamejaya) praises the Brahmin's narration of the Narayana story as unparalleled and purifying.
Janamejaya reflects on his ancestor Arjuna's victory with Krishna's help, emphasizing the power of allying with Vishnu.

extraction_text: Vaishampayana (the narrator) prepares to recount Narada's story after returning from White Island with Narayana's words.
Narada traveled a great distance safely from Mount Meru to Mount Gandhamadana and descended into the broad Badari hermitage.
Narada saw two ancient, excellent sages performing austerities in the hermitage.

attributes.description: The sages had divine characteristics including auspicious swastika marks, topknots, swan marks on arms, wheel marks on feet, broad shoulders, long arms, four testicles, sixty teeth, eight canines, handsome faces, broad foreheads, full cheeks, straight eyebrows and nose bridges, and heads like canopies.

extraction_text: Narada was pleased to see them, and they honored him, welcomed him, and inquired about his health.

Narada described how the residents of White Island, free from the five senses and awakened, worship the Supreme Person, who enjoys with them and loves devotees and Brahmins.
Narada described the Supreme God as worshipped, loving Bhagavata (Vishnu) devotees, enjoying with them, pervading everything, being creator, cause and effect, full of power and splendor.

relationships: Son of the Most High (likely Brahma)

extraction_text: Nara (那罗), the elder son of Dharma (正法之子), questioned Narada about whom he worships in these rituals and what fruits he expects.

extraction_text: Narada explained that he worships the eternal supreme soul, specifically Vishnu (毗湿奴/毗恭吒), as the highest sacrifice, following teachings received.
Narada revealed his lineage: Brahma (梵天) emerged from Vishnu, Brahma happily created his father Daksha (陀刹), and Narada himself was born from Brahma's mind.
Narada stated he worships ancestors according to rules established by Narayana (那罗延), who is the father, mother, and ancestor of the world, and he worships this world-lord in ancestral rites.
Narada described the transmission of Vedas where fathers forgot them and learned from sons, making sons become fathers in knowledge, and noted mutual respect between fathers and sons.
Narada asked about the origin of the title 'rice-ball' (饭团) used in rituals with kusha grass.

Nara and Narayana explained that when the earth disappeared into the ocean, Vishnu (乔宾陀) incarnated as a boar (野猪), pulled out the earth, and restored it, getting covered in mud and water while serving the world.

relationships: Nara and Narayana as divine explainers

extraction_text: The god (identified as Vishnu/Varaha) uses his tusk to pick up mud and places it on darbha grass at noon prayer time.
Vishnu pours his self into the mud lumps and performs ancestral rites according to rules, creating three lumps.
Vishnu faces east and scatters sesame with oil juice produced from his body's heat to complete the ritual.
Vishnu declares he creates the ancestors himself as world creator to establish rules.
The three mud lumps fall from the tusk to the southern ground and become ancestors while Vishnu contemplates the highest ancestral rites.
Vishnu declares the three formless lumps should forever be ancestors in the world, with himself as father, grandfather, and great-grandfather within them.
Vishnu questions who is higher than him and who he should worship, declaring himself as grandfather, ancestor, and cause.
Vishnu worships himself by offering the mud lumps on the boar mountain (Varaha Parvata) and disappears.
According to Vishnu's words, ancestors become known as pindas (rice balls) and are forever worshipped.
Worshipping ancestors, gods, teachers, guests, cows, excellent brahmins, and Mother Earth is equivalent to worshipping Vishnu, who resides equally in all beings as the great soul Narayana.

relationships: Vishnu as immanent in all worship
